subsystems.name: Positional chemistry tools
subsystems.role: hold reactant molecules at a precise position and angle so a bond forms only where it is wanted.
parts: nanolithographic patterning to place anchor sites

subsystems.name: Molecular building blocks
subsystems.role: the programmable parts that fold or bond in predictable ways.

subsystems.name: Assembly stages and fixtures
subsystems.role: the surface or scaffold a product is built on, because a free-swimming builder cannot hold position against Brownian motion.

subsystems.name: Coordination and control
subsystems.role: tells each unit what to make and catches mistakes.
parts: molecular signalling such as DNA strand displacement

subsystems.name: Energy and feedstock supply
subsystems.role: delivers precursor molecules and the energy that drives each bond-forming step.
parts: local energy input — heat, light, electrons or chemical potential

subsystems.name: Product extraction and scale-up
subsystems.role: removes finished structures and multiplies the number of working units.
parts: replication of the building units themselves

buildSteps.title: Pick a target chemistry
buildSteps.detail: Choose the product and the exact bonds to make. Only a narrow set of reactions can be driven positionally, so most materials are out of reach at the start.

buildSteps.title: Make the tools
buildSteps.detail: Fabricate atomically sharp probe tips and functionalise them with a catalytic group, or design DNA strands that fold into a jig holding two reactants together.

buildSteps.title: Make the feedstock
buildSteps.detail: Synthesise and purify precursor molecules that react only when triggered — by a voltage pulse, a photon or a catalyst brought close.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the stage
buildSteps.detail: Clean an atomically flat substrate in vacuum and pattern it with addressable anchor sites so each position on the workpiece has a known coordinate.

buildSteps.title: Assemble, step by step
buildSteps.detail: Bring the tip to a site, deposit one reactive group, move to the next site and repeat — or let complementary strands hybridise so many positions fill in at once.

buildSteps.title: Verify each structure
buildSteps.detail: Image with scanning probes and check with mass spectrometry; at this scale a single misplaced atom can ruin the function.

buildSteps.title: Release and purify
buildSteps.detail: Cleave the finished molecule from its anchor, harvest it and separate it from failed copies.

buildSteps.title: Scale by parallelism, not by swarms
buildSteps.detail: Free-floating nanobots cannot hold station in a liquid, so the practical route is thousands of fixed parallel assembly stations on one chip, with redundancy to tolerate failures.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Only if the units could build copies of themselves would output grow exponentially. This self-replication step is the hardest and most speculative part of the idea.

prerequisites.why: individual atoms have been positioned with scanning tunnelling microscopes since 1989 and single bonds formed and broken under a probe tip, but only a few operations per second, one at a time.
DNA synthesis is routine and DNA origami builds precise two- and three-dimensional shapes; extending that precision to arbitrary materials is unsolved.
ribosomes and virus capsids assemble with high fidelity, but synthetic systems are far simpler and less reliable.
there is no practical way to coordinate millions of independent units or to give them a shared plan.
bond-by-bond assembly needs an astronomical number of operations per gram of product, and each step costs energy.
most mechanosynthesis work happens in ultra-high vacuum and often at cryogenic temperatures, far from factory conditions.

pathway.milestone: single-molecule mechanosynthesis in vacuum; DNA nanotechnology making static nanostructures
pathway.unlocks: proof that atoms can be placed deliberately and that molecules can self-assemble into designed shapes.

pathway.milestone: parallel probe arrays and automated synthesis of small sequence-defined molecules
pathway.unlocks: throughput in the thousands of units rather than one at a time.

pathway.milestone: self-assembling systems that build working devices — sensors, catalysts, drug carriers — with built-in error correction
pathway.unlocks: useful nanoscale products without controlling every atom positionally.

pathway.milestone: hybrid factories using biomimetic assembly lines to make bulk atomically precise materials
pathway.unlocks: real quantities of strong, precisely structured polymers and composites.

pathway.milestone: self-replicating assemblers building macroscopic products bottom-up
pathway.unlocks: the original vision, if the control, energy and replication problems are ever solved.
